idiom_name: manual sealed cookie: serializer plus OpenSSL EVP MAC/AEAD behind a SessionCodec interface, written with the HTTP library's Set-Cookie header
implementation_notes: As in C there is no session facility, so the classic structure is assembled: a serializer (or a hand-written codec) turns the session object into a compact record, OpenSSL's EVP operations authenticate it (EVP_DigestSign* with an HMAC key) and optionally seal it (EVP_EncryptInit_ex with GCM), and the HTTP framework of choice writes the Set-Cookie header; the browser's ~4 KB per-cookie limit and the cookie grammar still apply. C++'s real advantage here is RAII: wrap EVP_MD_CTX and EVP_PKEY in owning types so a rejected request cannot leak handles on the early-return path, and hide the whole thing behind a SessionCodec interface so handlers see a typed session object. The hand-written form stays justified when you must control the wire format or interoperate with an existing token; otherwise a framework that already performs cookie cryptography is cheaper and safer.
pitfalls: EVP_MD_CTX and EVP_PKEY must be released on every path, including verification failure; without RAII wrappers the error path leaks on each rejected request.
The decoded payload stays untrusted after a successful MAC: parse with checked conversions and never trust client-supplied offsets or lengths.
base64url versus standard base64 and the cookie grammar (no semicolons, commas or whitespace in values) bite as soon as a second component writes the same cookie.
